title: GPU runtime deep dive: cache thrashing & kernel switch profiling
summary: Deep technical session focused on recurrent latency spikes NovaLabs observed under mixed-load inference. We walked through kernel-selection triggers that cause path switches, how CUDA-graph replay interacts with a persistent KV cache and provokes eviction/thrashing, and tradeoffs when moving from a vLLM software path to TRT-LLM kernels. Agreed next steps: run deterministic replay benchmarks, collect NVTX traces, and try a small TRT-LLM pilot on a reserved instance with tuned batching/quant profiles.
transcript:
Meeting Header:
- Date/Time: 2027-08-19 15:00 PDT
- Duration: 58 minutes
- Attendees: Samira Khan (Redwood AE), Ethan Brooks (Redwood SE), Marta Ruiz (NovaLabs CTO), Jordan Lee (ML Eng), Deepak Patel (Infra)
- Record link: https://redwood.internal/meetings/ff-20270819-001 (shared)

Summary (auto):
Samira opens with observed latency tail; customer describes intermittent 120-400ms token spikes vs baseline 40-60ms. Conversation drills into kernel selection heuristics, then CUDA-graph replay interactions with KV cache and eviction behavior. We cover quantization accuracy checks and safe batching configs for their VPC private deployment.

Topics: kernel heuristics; cuda-graph replay; kv cache prefetch/evict; trt-llm vs vllm; quant/batching; on-prem VPC setup.

Transcript:
[00:00] Samira (Redwood AE): okay, hi everyone thanks for joining we'll aim for 45-60 mins. quick intro, ethan is our runtime SE, he ran the profiling on the trace you shared. Marta, Jordan, Deepak, thanks for sending the nvtx dumps and those perf logs.
[00:25] Marta (NovaLabs): yeah thanks, we've been hitting these spikes in prod-like load, mostly multimodal chat asks, but really see it with long context. baseline is like 40-60ms per token, but every so often we get 120-400.
[00:40] Ethan (Redwood SE): and the spikes line up with kernel path switches in the trace. there are times the runtime falls back from the fast fused matmul kernel to a slower kernel set — we think because of sequence-length driven heuristics and a cudagraph replay mismatch.
[01:12] Jordan (NovaLabs): can you explain that mismatch? our infra team doesn't understand why cuda-graph replay would affect kv cache hit rate. it should just replay the same ops, right?
[01:30] Ethan: right, so the nuance — when you build a cuda-graph the runtime records kernels for a hot path, including assumptions about tensor shapes and sometimes predictive kv cache behavior. if there is an eviction or a prefetched KV chunk not present at replay time, or if the sequence length differs, the kernel selection logic can choose fallback kernels. that triggers micro-regression and longer latency.
[02:05] Deepak (NovaLabs): hmm, we've been reusing a persistent kv cache across sessions to save tokens but maybe our eviction policy is too aggressive. we configured LRU with a small bucket per GPU to keep mem low.
[02:26] Ethan: LRU is common but if cuda-graph replay expects a persistent kv layout it can assume addresses — so evictions that shift offsets can produce a non-matching graph replay and then the runtime invalidates the fast path. it's a kinda subtle memory-address/stride dependency.
[03:00] Samira: worth noting this is more pronounced on quantized kernels. quantized matmul kernels are more brittle to shape/stride changes because they inline packed tensors, so small layout shifts will lose the fused kernel benefits and fall back to generic kernels — heavier.
[03:28] Marta: that's interesting, we did a 4-bit per-channel quant run for cost reasons; maybe that's causing more of the spikes. we have seen quality OK but didn't correlate with latency.
[03:45] Ethan: exactly, quant reduces memory but increases kernel coupling. also TRT-LLM's fused kernels handle certain packing patterns better than the vLLM path in our tests, but TRT-LLM is strict about stable shapes. vLLM is more permissive but slower in the hot path sometimes.
[04:15] Jordan: so practically, is the advice to either tighten eviction so kv is stable, or to avoid cuda-graph replay? which is more pragmatic for us on-prem?
[04:33] Ethan: depends on your cost vs latency goals. option A: stabilize KV layout — increase cache size or change eviction window so repopulation is less frequent. option B: avoid long-lived cuda-graph replay for variable-length sessions — use short graphs or disable replay for the problematic route. option C: use TRT-LLM with careful warmup to ensure stable shapes — but that requires a calibration phase.
[05:10] Deepak: we run in a private VPC with limited GPU pool and have NVLink between two A100s. is there anything about multi-gpu nvlink that would amplify these issues?
[05:27] Ethan: yes, cross-gpu KV sharding adds coordination. if one GPU evicts a shard and the other expects it, you'll see stalls while the runtime synchronizes or falls back to remote-fetch kernels. nvlink helps but doesn't eliminate the cost.
[05:55] Samira: to add — we saw in the customer's traces that kernel switching often follows an all-gpu barrier where one device had to rebuild a KV slice. the runtime then chooses a conservative kernel set across the board leading to the whole inference lane slowing down.
[06:20] Jordan: are there instrumentation knobs we can flip to detect when the fallback happens? we have traces but not an easy alert.
[06:35] Ethan: yes, NVTX markers are the best quick-win. Redwood's trace collector can annotate kernel-choices: fused_matmul_fast vs fused_matmul_generic vs kv_remote_fetch. we'll share a small script to parse the nvprof/nvtx outputs.
[07:02] Marta: great. second question — TRT-LLM sounded promising in your benchmark doc but we're worried about dev ops complexity and reproducibility across our on-prem clusters.
[07:18] Samira: pragmatic approach is to run a small TRT pilot on a reservation instance mirroring your NVLink config. TRT-LLM gives better steady-state latency for stable shapes and heavy quant, but it's less forgiving on dynamic lengths. we'll run runs with your tokens and send back the tuned config.
[07:42] Deepak: and how does batching factor in? we've been using dynamic batching at the gateway with a 20ms latency cap. if we tune batcher size up or down, will that change kernel selection?
[07:57] Ethan: yes, batching affects tensor shapes and can push kernels into different code paths. continuous batching (variable batch sizes) increases shape diversity which can kill the fast fused kernels. recommendation: constrain the most latency-sensitive endpoints to fixed batch sizes or use padding to align shapes, or use a small batching window but deterministic shape padding.
[08:34] Jordan: padding sounds wasteful but might be better than periodic 300ms spikes.
[08:40] Samira: exactly, those tradeoffs are central. we can model cost impact.
[09:00] Speaker 6 (background): (inaudible)
[10:12] Ethan: quick aside on CUDA graphs — the runtime's current replay strategy assumes repeatable address mappings for some temp buffers. if the backend allocator uses jemalloc vs tcmalloc or has ASLR-like behavior, graph replay can produce mismatches. in our internal tests we saw that switching to a deterministic allocator reduced mismatches by ~70%.
[10:50] Marta: interesting, we're on a distro with default allocator; not tuned. is configuring allocator a supported knob in the private deployment?
[11:02] Samira: yes, in Redwood Private we surface allocator choice and recommend a deterministic allocator for heavy cuda-graph usage. we'll share recommended sysctl and docker run flags.
[11:20] Jordan: can you also share the concrete metrics we should watch? token latency p50/p95/p99? memory Bandwidth? Something that indicates early warnings before full tail spikes.
[11:35] Ethan: p95 and p99 token latency are the obvious. also nvlink stall counters, kernel fallback counts (we'll show how to parse), and KV eviction rate per minute. if eviction rate jumps, that's a leading indicator.
[12:10] Deepak: let's talk about quantization — you mentioned 4-bit per-channel earlier. we currently have a baseline 8-bit and experimented with 4-bit QAT. are there specific kernels that degrade faster with 4-bit?
[12:30] Ethan: per-channel 4-bit packing benefits memory but many fused kernels expect word-aligned packed tiles; misaligned packing (due to padding or odd sequence lengths) forces a deoptim path. TRT's kernels are often optimized for those packed layouts and can be faster, but they require strict layout stability.
[12:58] Marta: so if we want to keep 4-bit to save cost, what's the checklist to avoid thrash?
[13:10] Samira: checklist: 1) ensure per-GPU cache budgets are sized to avoid frequent evictions; 2) use deterministic allocator and consistent warmup sequences; 3) avoid unconstrained variable-length batching for latency-critical routes; 4) run NVTX tracing for a week during soak to gather representative shape distribution; 5) if using TRT-LLM, do a calibration phase with your representative prompts.
[13:50] Jordan: sounds good. any quick wins we can implement in the next sprint?
[13:57] Ethan: yes — increase KV cache target by 15% for the slow lane, add NVTX markers at request entry/exit, and instrument eviction counters. that's low-risk.
[14:12] Marta: we'll try that.
[14:22] Samira: also, we'll provide an example of short cuda-graph windows — instead of building one graph for entire conversation, build per-chunk graphs so variations don't cause global fallback.
[14:38] Deepak: are there known regressions in our current runtime version with CUDA 12.1 vs 12.3? we saw a note in the changelog.
[14:48] Ethan: yeah 12.3 changed some allocator behavior. we had one customer report more graph mismatches until they pinned a deterministic allocator. not always reproducible but it's a risk.
[15:05] Jordan: good to know.
[15:12] Samira: do we want to talk about telemetry and the Redwood console side briefly? we can expose kernel-level breakdowns per model route.
[15:20] Ethan: yes; console can show per-token kernel type distribution, p50/p99, evictions, and per-model batch shape heatmaps. that helps spot why certain prompts cause falls to slow kernels.
[15:40] Marta: can the console correlate prompt hash to kernel path? sometimes a user prompt set causes it.
[15:48] Samira: we hash prompt shapes and top-k tokens, and you can link prompt hash to traces in the console. we won't store prompt text unless you enable pii-safe logging — default is shape-only.
[16:10] Jordan: excellent. a few more clarifying Qs: 1) what's the expected overhead of NVTX markers? 2) is there a Redwood agent to collect traces from on-prem?
[16:25] Ethan: 1) NVTX negligible if you only annotate entry/exit and kernel switches; heavy sampling adds CPU overhead. 2) Yes, we have a small collector (sidecar) that uploads anonymized traces to your Redwood Console or to a private S3 — it's included in the Private package.
[16:48] Deepak: security question — if we share nvtx traces, do they ever contain PII? we scrub prompt content, but are there artifacts?
[17:00] Samira: good point. default collector mode scrubs strings and only sends shape/marker metadata and kernel names. we have an options doc for stricter scrub. we'll share security whitepaper.
[17:20] Marta: can we see an example NVTX + kernel sample from your earlier customer where you fixed the issue? real example helps.
[17:30] Ethan: yes we'll attach two examples: a bad trace with fallback and a post-fix trace where the kernel footprint is stable.
[17:42] Jordan: any other hardware considerations — like using HBM2e settings or running on L4 vs A100 — does behavior differ?
[17:54] Ethan: smaller GPUs with less HBM (like L4) can exacerbate eviction frequency; A100 with big HBM tolerates more caching. also NVLink matters for sharded KV: without fast interconnect you see more remote fetch fallbacks.
[18:12] Deepak: we have NVLink but we'll try increasing cache headroom on one GPU to see if that changes sync events.
[18:22] Samira: good test.
[18:30] -- brief silence / off topic scheduling chat --
[22:05] Ethan: shifting to TRT vs vLLM comparison notes: vLLM path offers more graceful degradation for dynamic inputs and simpler debugging; TRT-LLM gives better throughput for steady shapes and heavy quant, but more brittle during live A/B traffic. choose TRT for steady production where you can strictly control warmup and shapes.
[22:40] Marta: we already A/B traffic internally; maybe we'll test TRT on a small route first.
[22:50] Samira: recommended pilot: 2-week pilot on a mirror route with 10% traffic, deterministic allocator, NVTX enabled, and a config that pins cache sizes. we'll produce the config.
[23:05] Jordan: fine.
[23:10] Ethan: quick note: when using TRT-LLM with 4-bit quant, do an accuracy sweep vs your eval prompts. some prompt patterns (long tables) push packed tiles out-of-alignment and change logits subtly. we have an eval harness you can reuse.
[23:36] Marta: can you share that harness?
[23:40] Samira: yes, we will.
[24:00] -- later: action item recap --
[24:10] Samira: recap: Redwood will share: 1) benchmark template and a trace parsing script (NVTX -> kernel-fallback counts), 2) cuda-graph debug runbook and deterministic allocator recommendations, 3) example traces (pre/post fix), 4) TRT pilot config and eval harness. NovaLabs will: run increased KV headroom test, enable NVTX markers, and run the 2-week pilot on a mirror route if pilot config looks good.
[24:45] Marta: yep, we'll start with the KV headroom test this week.
[25:00] Deepak: what's the timeline for Redwood to send artifacts?
[25:05] Samira: by EOD Tuesday 2027-08-24 we'll send the bench template and runbook.
[25:12] Jordan: thanks.
[25:20] Samira: ok last Qs?
[25:30] Marta: none from me.
[25:33] Jordan: nope.
[25:35] Samira: great thanks all. we'll schedule follow-up check-in after you run the headroom test.
[25:42] Ethan: thanks everyone.
[25:45] (meeting ends)
